_about: Mars overlay, deep-merged over data/text.json (arrays replace). Owners: campaign and screens (M4) everything here except survey, instruments and drill (milestones and survey, M5). Integration (M6) wires the sol, night and storm strings into the HUD; they may use the {placeholders} of missionVars() in src/ui/tutorialText.ts. Every real fact cites its source (historySources, campaign.sources).

partText._about: Mars wording for the shared parts (data/parts.json), by part id; numbers stay the Moon's. Mars-only parts carry their wording in data/parts.json itself. Matches the Mars rules: no driving at night without lights, map-wide night cold, solar income by day only and less in a dust storm, soft ground only in Seitah's sand ripples.

wheels-solid.description: Cheap and heavy. Lower grip in sand ripples.

power-fixed-panel.description: A flat panel. Solar income by day, most with the Sun high. Nothing at night, less in a dust storm.

power-solar-mast.description: Twice the fixed panel's solar income. Nothing at night, less in a dust storm. Light, expensive and bulky.

lights-led.description: Lets the rover keep driving at night, at a high battery cost.

heater-none.description: Saves cost, mass, and space. Without another source of heat the rover freezes in its first night.

heater-rhu.description: Steady heat from decaying isotopes. Lets the rover survive the night cold.

instrument-drill.name: Rock drill
instrument-drill.description: Drills rock cores. Heavier and bulkier than the camera.

slots._note: Names of the support slots Mars offers (data/mars/parts.json supportSlots), merged into the shared slot names. Since November 16 the arm and the mast are payload systems in the bay; these names are kept for the parts' slots.

support._note: Support hardware on the desk (Mars M5): an instrument whose support part is missing is refused with a reason. {support}: the support part's name below; {part}: the instrument. The arm as the X-ray's optional upgrade (game-design.md, The X-ray spectrometer and the robotic arm; ui/supportText.ts armNotes, ui/milestoneText.ts rewardText, ui/missionScreen.ts finishXray): xrayWithArm on the X-ray's card and armAdds on the arm's ({reach}: tuning.instruments.arm.reachM), groundDown on the mission's first ground-down X-ray reading and groundDownReward after a raised milestone reward ({percent}: from groundDownFactor). Lesson-blind: no word about slopes or level ground.

support.xrayWithArm: With the robotic arm: reaches about {reach} m and grinds the rock surface first, so readings earn more.

landing.heading: Landing: Jezero crater
landing.briefing: The lander has touched down on the floor of Jezero crater on Mars. The crater is about 45 km wide and held a lake, fed by a river that built a delta, about 3.5 billion years ago. The rover is deploying.

ticket.briefing: REL secures a spot for the rover on the next commercial launch to Mars. The lander will set it down on the floor of Jezero crater.

nightBudget._note: The spec sheet's night tile (Mars M15; game-design.md, the night budget line): the battery's net rate at night for this build, per second, asleep and parked awake with the lights on (draw minus an RTG's income), with the whole night's net change underneath (and, for an amber or red value, its share of the battery, the words in the tooltip), coloured by state; the value's unit is design.spec.perSecond, as on the Charging tile. The tooltip and screen-reader sentence give both scales, the night's length, the draws, the electric heater's share and the RTG's income. Numbers from data (rules/energy.ts nightBudget, nightNetState). Shown once the power source is chosen. Lesson-blind: nothing says a rover needs lights or a heater.

nightBudget.changesLights: {rate} per second awake with lights ({net} over a night)
nightBudget.stateLarge: {mode}: one night uses {percent}% of the battery.
nightBudget.stateEmpties: {mode}: one night would empty the battery.

watch.tip: A regional dust storm reaches the site partway through the mission. An orbital forecast warns about {stormLeadSols} sol ahead.
Each of the {sols} sols ends in a night with no sunlight, and the rover cools everywhere on the map.
Séítah's sand ripples are soft. A heavy rover sinks in and can get stuck.
Hard impacts and ground steeper than {maxSlope}° damage the rover, and a rollover ends the mission.

science.text: Rock layers at the delta front
science.tip: Jezero's ancient river delta exposes layers laid down in and around the old lake.
Each site has its own rocks, and the foot of the delta holds rock from the old lake.
What lies under the crater floor can be imaged from the surface.
Pressure, wind and dust in the air change from day to night and through the storm.
Some ground holds more hydrogen than the ground around it.

design.overTopTier: Exceeds the Heavy ticket limits. The rover cannot launch.
speedInfo: The mission compresses {sols} sols on Mars into {minutes} minutes. Driving is compressed too: rovers in this game drive {compression} times faster than the real speeds their parts are modeled on.

On Apollo 15 in 1971, the crew reported that about 6 to 7 km/h was the most comfortable driving speed for the Lunar Roving Vehicle. Its top speed was of the order of 9 to 13 km/h, depending on slope, roughness, and soil.
Robotic rovers drive far slower. NASA's Curiosity and Perseverance rovers on Mars have a top speed of about 4 cm/s (0.15 km/h) on flat ground.

story.site: Mission 2 goes to Jezero crater on Mars. About 3.5 billion years ago the crater held a lake, fed by a river that built a delta at its edge. NASA's Perseverance rover landed here in 2021 and has drilled rock cores from that delta.
sources: NASA JPL, Mars 2020 Landing Press Kit: Landing Site (jpl.nasa.gov/news/press_kits/mars_2020/landing/mission/landing_site/)
NASA JPL, NASA's Perseverance Rover Investigates Geologically Rich Mars Terrain (jpl.nasa.gov/news/nasas-perseverance-rover-investigates-geologically-rich-mars-terrain/)

debrief.failedRound: The balance is below the pass mark for the next mission, Titan ({minimum}). The round must be restarted. Balance, research points and records return to their values at the start of the Mars round.
debrief.passedRound: The balance meets the pass mark for the next mission, Titan ({minimum}). The Mars round is complete.
debrief.storyPassed: The Jezero results fund the program's last mission: a rover for the Shangri-La dunes on Titan, Saturn's largest moon. Titan takes away the sunlight. The battery is the budget, and the cold never lets up.
debrief.storyFailed: On these results, REL cannot fund the mission to Titan. The board has approved another attempt at Jezero crater, and the engineering notebook keeps what this rover learned.

history.survived: NASA's Opportunity rover was designed for a 90-sol mission on Mars and kept working for more than 14 years, from its landing in January 2004 to its last signal on June 10, 2018.
history.froze: NASA's Spirit rover, embedded in soft soil since 2009, could not tilt itself toward the low winter Sun; without power for its survival heaters it likely became colder inside than in any earlier winter. Its last communication was on March 22, 2010.

historySources.survived: NASA, NASA's Record-Setting Opportunity Rover Mission on Mars Comes to End (www.nasa.gov/news-release/nasas-record-setting-opportunity-rover-mission-on-mars-comes-to-end)

comingSoon.heading: Titan: coming soon
comingSoon.body: The Mars mission is complete. The Titan mission is in development. Research points and the balance are banked for it.

design.title: Mission 2: Mars
body: The campaign continues on Mars, on the floor of Jezero crater. The balance carried over from the Moon is {balance}.

Mars has its own parts. The Moon's carry over, without the laser retroreflector and the seismometer station, which have no work to do on this mission. New are a radioisotope generator and deployable solar arrays, a larger battery, an electric heater, grouser wheels, a robotic arm and a mast for instruments that need them, and four Mars instruments. Launches to Mars have their own ticket tiers: {tiers}.

After the mission, the balance must stay at or above the pass mark for Titan ({nextMinimum}), or the Mars round is restarted. A restart returns the balance, research points and records to their values at the start of the Mars round.

design.title: Designing for the night
body: Each sol on Mars ends with a night. The solar panel earns nothing at night and less while the Sun is low, so the battery must carry the rover through every night.
With lights the rover can keep driving at night, but the lights drain the battery. Without lights it cannot drive at night and can only sleep until dawn.
Nights are cold everywhere on the map. A heater slows freezing; without one, the rover freezes quickly at night.

design.title: Power through the night
body: The specification sheet has a Night energy tile under the battery: how one {nightSeconds} s night changes this rover's battery, asleep and parked awake with its lights on. Choose a battery that holds more than a night's loss, with some left for the morning drive.

Solar power or steady power. The fixed panel and the solar mast earn by day only. The deployable solar arrays earn the most in sunlight, but they are bulky. A radioisotope generator (RTG) earns a steady trickle day and night, through the dust storm too, and its waste heat keeps the rover warm. It is expensive and heavy, and it earns no more in a sol than a fixed panel does on a clear sol.

Two heaters. Radioisotope heater units keep the rover warm and draw no energy. The electric heater is cheaper and lighter, but it draws on the battery every night, even while the rover sleeps; the Night energy tile includes its share. A rover with an RTG needs no other heater.

design.title: Dust storm
body: One regional dust storm reaches the site during the mission. For about {stormSols} sols, solar income falls to about {stormSolarPercent}%.
A larger battery, or a rover that can sleep through the storm, keeps the mission going.

design.title: Arm and mast
body: On Mars the payload bay also offers a robotic arm and a remote sensing mast. Each takes one mounting point, like any payload item. The organics spectrometer needs the robotic arm. The X-ray spectrometer works without it, as on the Moon; with the arm it reaches boulders farther away and grinds the rock surface first, so its readings earn more. The laser spectrometer needs the remote sensing mast, which also widens the camera's viewpoint photo zones. Leave them off when nothing aboard uses them.

drive.title: Sols on Mars
body: The mission lasts {minutes} minutes, which represent {sols} sols. Each sol is {daySeconds} s of daylight followed by {nightSeconds} s of night; the night is time-lapsed faster than the day. There is no clock: time is read from the Sun.
The solar panel earns most with the Sun high, less in the morning and evening, and nothing at night.

drive.title: Instruments

camera.name: Camera
camera.counts: Counts at the delta-front viewpoint, from a crater's rim facing its far inner wall, of a passing dust devil, and away from the lander facing west with the setting Sun low in the frame.

drill.name: Drill
drill.counts: Counts at several sites, each at least {stationMinDistance} m from the lander and {sampleSpacing} m from each other. Séítah and the foot of the delta hold rock of their own.

neutron.name: Neutron spectrometer
neutron.counts: The hydrogen meter reads the ground under the rover. Drive it through Séítah or along the delta front, and watch for ground where it reads higher than anywhere else.

xray.name: X-ray spectrometer
xray.counts: Each site has its own rocks; the readout says when a type is new.

weather.name: Weather mast
weather.counts: Left on more than {stationMinDistance} m from the lander, it records the dust storm, part of a night while the rover is awake, and dust devils nearby. It can forecast the storm before the orbital report.

radar.name: Radar
radar.counts: Keep it on for long drives more than {stationMinDistance} m from the lander, past young craters, Séítah or the delta front, to image their buried layers.

laser.name: Laser spectrometer
laser.counts: The HUD shows the target: a boulder or the delta cliff.

organics.name: Organics spectrometer
organics.counts: The reading uses a lot of energy, and the rover holds still until it ends.

drive.emptyBay: The payload bay is empty: this rover carries no instruments.
body: Each instrument has its number key and a button beside the meters.

drive.title: Night: lights on or sleep
body: At sunset a notice reads: "{sunsetNotice}"
Lights on: the rover keeps driving and can still earn milestones, but the lights drain the battery and the panel earns nothing.

Sleep: power down with P. The battery drains slowly, the rover cannot drive or earn milestones, and it wakes by itself at dawn. A rover that stays awake without driving still uses some power, so sleep is the cheapest choice.
A rover without lights cannot drive at night. If the battery runs out at night, the mission ends.

drive.title: Night cold and damage
body: Every night the cold meter rises, everywhere on the map, and it falls again by day. When it is full, the rover freezes. A heater slows freezing, and nights are milder during the dust storm.
Hard impacts and ground steeper than {maxSlope}° damage the rover, as on the Moon. Sand ripples are soft ground where the wheels can dig in.

drive.title: Dust storm forecast
body: An orbital weather report forecasts the dust storm about {stormLeadSols} sol before it arrives.
For about {stormSols} sols, solar income falls to about {stormSolarPercent}%. Charge the battery before it arrives, drive less, or sleep through it.

drive.title: Where to go first
body: The map starts zoomed in on the lander and widens as the rover explores. It shows only ground within {revealRadius} m of where the rover has been, and sites appear once the rover finds them. Arrows at the edge of the map point toward the orbital survey leads, each with its distance: the nearest lead is drawn larger and listed first under the map.

Start with the sites near the lander. Rocky area 2, an old crater with boulders on its rim, is about half a kilometer west-northwest. Small young craters lie about 0.6 km to the south, west-southwest and southwest, and Rocky area 1, a boulder field, about 0.7 km south. Séítah, East crater and the delta front are farther out, 1 to 1.5 km.
The engineering notebook records what the mission teaches about the rover. Open it with N or the Notebook button; the mission pauses while it is open, and Escape closes it.

terrainFallback: Terrain: USGS Mars 2020 Terrain Relative Navigation HiRISE and CTX elevation models of Jezero crater.
credits.imageryFallback: USGS Mars 2020 Terrain Relative Navigation HiRISE orthomosaic of Jezero crater.
credits._parts: Mars step 8: the real basis of the Mars parts, from the sources game-design.md (Mars rover design) and the Mars engineering plan (Real anchors) cite, via research/rover-engineering/02. Labels are the part names. No entry names a lesson: nothing about neutrons on the RTG, nothing about dust on the arrays, nothing about slopes on the arm. The remote sensing mast has no checked source, so it has none.

partEntries.label: Radioisotope generator (RTG)
partEntries.text: NASA's Curiosity and Perseverance rovers run on a Multi-Mission Radioisotope Thermoelectric Generator, which gives steady power day and night; its waste heat helps keep the rover warm.
partEntries.citation: NASA, Multi-Mission Radioisotope Thermoelectric Generator fact sheet; U.S. Department of Energy, Powering Curiosity: Multi-Mission Radioisotope Thermoelectric Generators

partEntries.label: Deployable solar arrays
partEntries.text: The solar panels of NASA's Spirit and Opportunity rovers folded up for landing and opened out to about 1.3 square meters.
partEntries.citation: NASA JPL, Mars Exploration Rover launch press kit (2003)

partEntries.label: Electric heater
partEntries.text: Spirit's and Opportunity's warm electronics box was kept warm by electric heaters, radioisotope heater units and the heat of the electronics themselves.
partEntries.citation: NASA JPL, Mars Exploration Rover launch press kit (2003)

partEntries.label: Larger battery pack
partEntries.text: Perseverance carries two lithium-ion batteries of about 43 ampere-hours each.
partEntries.citation: NASA JPL, Mars 2020 Perseverance landing press kit

partEntries.label: Grouser wheels
partEntries.text: Perseverance's aluminum wheels carry 48 grousers, with a skin about twice as thick as Curiosity's.
partEntries.citation: NASA JPL, Mars 2020 Perseverance landing press kit

partEntries.label: Robotic arm
partEntries.text: Perseverance's arm is about 2.1 m long; its turret holds the coring drill, PIXL, SHERLOC and the WATSON camera.
partEntries.citation: NASA JPL, Mars 2020 Perseverance landing press kit

credits.generated: The boulders and the dust devils are generated by the game's own rules, not taken from a data set. The flood boulder, the hydrated ground, the olivine rock at Rocky area 2 and each site's rock types are placed by design, inspired by the findings credited under the milestone facts; they were not observed at these spots. The young craters, Séítah's sand ripples and the delta front are found in the HiRISE terrain and imagery credited above.

survey._owner: M5. Lead ids match data/mars/tuning.json survey.leads. Directions and distances are computed, so the text names none.
survey._sources: Delta: Fassett and Head, GRL 32 (2005), doi.org/10.1029/2005GL023456. Seitah: NASA JPL, "NASA's Perseverance Rover Begins Its First Science Campaign on Mars" (jpl.nasa.gov/news/nasas-perseverance-rover-begins-its-first-science-campaign-on-mars/). HiRISE scale: uahirise.org/TRA_000823_1720; usgs.gov/news/mars-2020-mission-be-guided-usgs-astrogeology-maps. delta.name: Delta front
delta.source: Orbital images show the fan of an ancient river delta, first described as a delta built into a crater lake in 2005. Its front is a cliff where the layers are exposed.

seitah.name: Séítah
seitah.source: HiRISE images show ridged rock with sand ripples between the ridges; the ripples are soft ground. Séítah means "amidst the sand" in the Navajo language.

rocks.name: Boulder field
rocks.source: HiRISE images, at about 25 cm per pixel, show a rough patch of boulders on the crater floor.

youngCrater.name: Young crater
youngCrater.source: HiRISE images show a deep crater with a sharp, round rim strewn with blocks: a young crater, not yet worn down like the older craters around it.

survey._legend6c: Mars step 6c: legend entries for the new site kinds (each shows once such a site is on the map) and the distance under a lead arrow's number.
survey._siteNames: Display names for the terrain.json site names, which the pipeline keeps ASCII (shown in the Located notice).
survey._sites: Mars step 4b: notes and instrument lines for the data/mars/sites.json sites (rules/types.ts TextFile survey; ui/surveyText.ts foundNotice). They replace the Moon's by key (deep merge), so the Moon's fresh rocky area does not reach Mars; its cold-trap and rolled-boulder lines stay merged but Mars has no such sites. Lesson-blind: no line names slope, level, flat, steep, dust, noise, generator or lights (Mars sites plan, Spoiler guard). Notes for the knobs, the Seitah edge, the delta foot and the flood boulder are ready for the survey sites Mars step 5c adds.

instrumentText._note: Mars's own instruments (Mars M4, behavior built in Mars step 4a) and the organics spectrometer's slope refusal (the X-ray's until November 16; since then the X-ray reads on any drivable ground). Real facts use the safe wording of the Mars engineering plan's Real anchors (ranges, "signals consistent with"); each cites its source. Placeholders: rules/types.ts InstrumentText.

xray.fact: Perseverance's X-ray spectrometer, PIXL, sits on the rover's arm and maps the elements in small patches of rock. In Séítah it found a rock made of packed olivine crystals that settled out of a thick body of cooling magma.
xray.source: Liu et al. (2022), An olivine cumulate outcrop on the floor of Jezero crater, Mars, Science 377:1513-1519, doi:10.1126/science.abo2756

weather.notCarried: This rover carries no weather mast.
weather.forecast: Weather mast: the pressure and dust readings point to a regional dust storm reaching the site in about {sols} sols, before the orbital report. Solar income will fall to about {stormSolarPercent}%.
weather.forecastNoSolar: Weather mast: the pressure and dust readings point to a regional dust storm reaching the site in about {sols} sols, before the orbital report.
weather.log: Weather mast: recorded pressure and dust for {seconds} s.
weather.logStorm: It forecast the dust storm before the orbital report.
weather.fact: NASA's Perseverance rover carries MEDA, a set of weather sensors that measures pressure, temperature, wind, humidity and dust in the air at Jezero crater.
weather.source: Rodriguez-Manfredi et al. (2021), The Mars Environmental Dynamics Analyzer, MEDA, Space Science Reviews 217:48, doi:10.1007/s11214-021-00816-9

radar.notCarried: This rover carries no ground-penetrating radar.
radar.log: Ground-penetrating radar: longest unbroken profile {meters} m. Ground profiled: {layers}.
radar.fact: NASA's Perseverance rover carries RIMFAX, a ground-penetrating radar. Along the rover's drives it imaged rock layers beneath the floor of Jezero crater, some of them inclined rather than flat.
radar.source: Hamran et al. (2022), Science Advances, doi:10.1126/sciadv.abp8564; UCLA news release, August 25, 2022 (www.college.ucla.edu/2022/08/25/mars-underground-images-from-perseverance-rover)

laser.notCarried: This rover carries no laser spectrometer.
laser.holding: Laser reading. The rover holds still.
laser.noTarget: {name}: nothing to read ahead. Face a boulder or the delta cliff within {reach} m.
laser.target: Laser target: {target}, {distance} m. Press {key} to read it.
laser.resultCliff: Laser reading of the delta cliff: fine layers of sedimentary rock.
laser.fact: The laser of SuperCam, on NASA's Perseverance rover, analyzes rocks up to about 7 m away.

organics.notCarried: This rover carries no organics spectrometer.
organics.holding: Organics reading. The rover holds still.
organics.target: Boulder within reach. Stop and press {key} for an organics reading.
organics.slope: {name}: the ground here is too steep for the arm ({slope}°). The arm reads on ground up to {max}°.
organics.result: Organics reading complete. The rock's spectrum is stored for scientists on Earth.
organics.stopped: {name}: reading stopped. The battery could not pay for the rest of it.
organics.log: Organics spectrometer: finished readings: {count}. Spectra stored.
organics.fact: SHERLOC, on NASA's Perseverance rover, detected signals consistent with organic molecules in rocks on the floor of Jezero crater. It identified no specific compounds, and sources other than life are not ruled out.
organics.source: Sharma et al. (2023), Diverse organic-mineral associations in Jezero crater, Mars, Nature 619:724-732, doi:10.1038/s41586-023-06143-z

instruments._owner: M5: Mars overrides of the shared instrument notices, plus the sunset notices (rules/marsTypes.ts MarsInstrumentText).
instruments.photoNoZone: Photograph added to the album. Milestones count at viewpoints, from a crater rim toward its far wall, with a dust devil or the setting Sun low in view, or close to a boulder already read.
instruments.captionDustDevil: Dust devil crossing the crater floor
instruments.sunsetHint: The setting Sun is low in view. Press {key} to take a photograph.
instruments.sunsetTooHigh: The Sun is in view but still high. The sunset photo counts once it is within {max}° of the horizon.
instruments.sunsetTooClose: The setting Sun is in view, but the rover is only {distance} m from the lander. The sunset photo counts at least {min} m away.

_rocks: Mars rock types (Mars step 4b; game-design.md, Mars rock types; ids in rules/marsTypes.ts MARS_ROCK_IDS). Merged with the Moon's names by id; Mars suites name only these. Readouts are plain words, as the X-ray and laser results show them. Sources: Farley et al. 2022 (Maaz, Seitah); Liu et al. 2022 (olivine cumulate); Tice et al. 2022 (carbonate in Seitah's olivine); Scheller et al. 2022 (salts from brines); Mangold et al. 2021 (delta lake layers, flood boulders). Flood conglomerate is placed by design.
